title: Reaction Kinetics
short_title: collision theory, activation energy, catalysts and rate
standard_text: Reactants must collide to react, and the reaction rate depends on the surrounding conditions: collision theory, factors affecting rate, activation energy, potential energy diagrams, catalysts and reaction mechanisms. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Chemistry 12)
meta_desc: Free Chemistry 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): collision theory, activation energy, catalysts and rate. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation.
key_sub: A catalyst lowers the activation energy.
body_html:
How to think about it

Collision theory: a reaction happens only when particles collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and the right orientation. Higher temperature, higher concentration, greater surface area and catalysts all increase the rate.

A potential energy diagram shows the energy of reactants, products and the activated complex. A catalyst provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy and is not used up. A reaction mechanism is a series of steps; the slowest step decides the overall rate.

Example

Why does powdered sugar burn faster than a sugar cube?

More surface for collisions

Answer: greater surface area

Example

Does a catalyst change ΔH?

It changes only the path.

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a catalyst is used up.
  • Thinking temperature only increases the number of collisions (it also increases their energy).
  • Thinking a catalyst shifts equilibrium.

faq.a: The slowest step in a reaction mechanism.

faq.q: Why do foods last longer in the fridge?
faq.a: Lower temperature slows the reactions that spoil food.

items.q: What happens to the yield of ammonia if ammonia is removed as it forms?
c: the equilibrium shifts right, so more ammonia forms
items.e: Removing a product makes the system replace it.

items.q: One large lump of zinc is used instead of zinc granules. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Less surface area means fewer collisions.

items.q: Increasing the concentration of a reactant…
c: increases the rate because collisions are more frequent
items.e: More particles in the same volume.

items.q: What happens to the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve at a higher temperature?
c: the curve starts at a higher energy
the peak moves to the left and gets higher
the area under the curve increases
the peak moves to the right and gets lower
items.e: More molecules have higher energies, but the total number is the same.

items.q: Why does powdered marble react faster with acid than marble chips?
c: the powder has a larger surface area, so more collisions happen
items.e: Only surface particles can collide.

items.q: Charcoal is burned as large lumps instead of small pieces. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.
A catalyst gives a path with lower activation energy.
Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: Why do most collisions not lead to a reaction?
c: the particles do not have enough energy or the right orientation
items.e: Successful collisions need E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>.

items.q: What happens to the rate of a gas reaction if the pressure is doubled?
c: it increases, because the particles are closer together
items.e: Higher pressure means higher concentration of gas.

items.q: In a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, what does the area under the curve represent?
items.e: The area stays the same when the temperature changes.

items.q: A catalyst is added to H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2HI (making hydrogen iodide) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the right
the equilibrium shifts to the left
the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: Which factor changes the value of K<sub>c</sub>?
items.e: K<sub>c</sub> depends only on temperature.

items.q: What is the activation energy?
c: the minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen
the average kinetic energy of the molecules
the energy released by a reaction
items.e: Collisions with less energy do not react.

items.q: A catalyst is added to PCl<sub>5</sub> ⇌ PCl<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> (phosphorus pentachloride dissociating) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
the equilibrium shifts to the right
the equilibrium shifts to the left
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: Why does the rate of reaction decrease as the reaction goes on?
c: reactants are used up, so their concentration falls
items.e: The curve levels off when a reactant runs out.

items.q: A catalyst is added. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: A catalyst gives a path with lower activation energy.

items.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of reaction?
c: it is used up in the reaction
it provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
it gives particles more kinetic energy
items.e: The catalyst is unchanged at the end.

items.q: A catalyst is added to N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (the Haber process) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the right
the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
the equilibrium shifts to the left
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: A more concentrated acid is used. Which explains the change in rate?
c: More particles in the same volume collide more often.
A catalyst gives a path with lower activation energy.
Fewer particles per volume means fewer collisions.
Less surface area means fewer collisions.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: Why are enzymes important industrial catalysts?
c: they work at low temperatures and are very specific, saving energy
they work only at high temperature
items.e: Enzymes are used in detergents and food processing.

items.q: According to collision theory, what must happen for particles to react?
c: they must collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) and the right orientation
they must be in the same phase
items.e: Only a fraction of collisions are successful.

items.q: Why does increasing concentration increase the rate of reaction?
c: there are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
items.e: Rate depends on collision frequency.

items.q: How can the rate of the reaction between magnesium and acid be measured?
c: measure the pH once at the end
measure the colour of the acid
measure the volume of hydrogen made every 10 seconds
items.e: A gas syringe collects the gas.

items.q: How does a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve change at a higher temperature?
c: the area under the curve doubles
the peak moves to the right and lowers, and more particles are above Ea
the peak moves left and rises
items.e: The total number of particles stays the same.

items.q: The acid is heated from 20 °C to 40 °C. Which explains the change in rate?
c: More surface area exposes more particles to collisions.
Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy.
Higher oxygen concentration means more collisions.
Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: A campfire is fanned to supply more oxygen. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Higher oxygen concentration means more collisions.

items.q: A catalyst is added to CH<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CO + 3H<sub>2</sub> (steam reforming) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the left
the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
the equilibrium shifts to the right
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: Charcoal is burned as large lumps instead of small pieces. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.

items.q: On a graph of volume of gas against time, what does a steeper slope mean?

items.e: Rate = gradient of the curve.

items.q: The gas is squeezed into a smaller container. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Higher pressure packs gas particles closer, so they collide more often.
Fewer particles per volume means fewer collisions.
Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: Why are catalytic converters fitted to car exhausts?
c: they speed up the conversion of CO, NO and unburnt fuel into less harmful gases
items.e: They contain platinum, palladium and rhodium.

items.q: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of reaction?
c: more particles have energy above the activation energy, and they collide more often
items.e: The effect on energy is the bigger one.

items.q: The gas is squeezed into a smaller container. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Higher pressure packs gas particles closer, so they collide more often.

items.q: The reaction mixture is stirred constantly. Which explains the change in rate?
c: More surface area exposes more particles to collisions.
Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.
Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy.
Stirring brings fresh reactant particles together.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann diagram, how does a catalyst change the picture?
c: the activation energy line moves to the left, so more particles have enough energy
items.e: The distribution itself does not change.

items.q: What does 'dynamic equilibrium' mean?
c: there are equal amounts of reactants and products
the forward and backward rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant
items.e: It needs a closed system.

items.q: What is Le Chatelier's principle?
c: equilibrium always lies to the right
a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change in conditions
pressure has no effect on gases
items.e: Use it to predict the effect of changing temperature, pressure or concentration.

items.q: Which part of the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve shows the molecules that can react?
c: the area to the right of the activation energy

items.q: A campfire is fanned to supply more oxygen. Which explains the change in rate?

items.q: A more concentrated acid is used. What happens to the reaction rate?

items.q: Why is the Haber process run at about 450 °C even though a lower temperature gives a higher yield?

it is a compromise that gives a fast enough rate
items.e: A low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction but is too slow.
